svg.title: Making time for a shared activity

text.tspan: Everyday English - C2 - 2026/06/21 - Essay - 01
A family spends time together.
Pexels · 5276077
Making time for a shared activity
To spend time with someone who cares for us is to negotiate a familiar but frequently obscured relationship between intentional design and the
contingencies of shared experience. The question is not whether arrangements are desirable, but what authority they should acquire. A credible position
supports preparation while withholding the assumption that procedural coherence is equivalent to human value.
There is a substantive case for structure: a simple shared activity creates space for conversation. Here, we choose a short walk that suits everyone’s
pace. The arrangement earns its legitimacy through the specific difficulty it alleviates, not through its conformity to an abstract ideal of order. Its success is
consequently conditional. Once the intervention demands more attention than the obstacle it removes, the original justification begins to unravel.
An assessment confined to that practical benefit would nevertheless be incomplete, since attention matters more than an elaborate plan. In concrete
terms, we put our phones away and ask about a familiar memory. This introduces a problem of perspective: whose convenience supplies the standard
against which improvement is measured? An apparently neutral procedure may privilege the preferences of its designer. Attentiveness to others makes
that asymmetry visible and creates grounds for revision.
What emerges is a qualified defence of planning, rather than a celebration of either control or spontaneity. Arrangements can sustain an experience
without exhausting its meaning. Their authority should remain answerable to the people and circumstances they affect; otherwise, a means of making life
more habitable risks becoming the criterion to which life must conform.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each body paragraph
needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
Persuade a group to change how they spend time with someone who cares for us. Support your recommendation with two different reasons and a
practical example of each. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion. (Model: One possible outline: introduce the
situation; discuss a simple shared activity creates space for conversation with an example; discuss attention matters more than an elaborate plan with a
different example; conclude by connecting the two points.)
